The textbook establishes that when multiple forces act on an object, their scalar components must be resolved along perpendicular axes (east as positive x-axis, north as positive y-axis), then combined to find the resultant; for the toy to remain stationary, an equilibrating force must be antiparallel to this resultant, meaning it points in the opposite direction with equal magnitude. The direction of a force vector is determined by the signs of its scalar components—both negative components indicate the vector lies in the third quadrant (south of west).

This subsection introduces kinetic energy, the energy of motion, defined for a particle as KE = ½mv², where m is mass and v is speed. The textbook establishes that kinetic energy can alternatively be expressed in terms of momentum as KE = p²/(2m), since p = mv, and that for a system of particles, total kinetic energy is found by summing the kinetic energies of all constituent particles. Classical kinetic energy applies at non-relativistic speeds (much less than the speed of light), while relativistic speeds require different expressions from special relativity. The units of kinetic energy are joules (kg·m²/s²), identical to the units of work, because work and kinetic energy represent different forms of the same fundamental physical property. Key searchable entities: kinetic energy, energy of motion, mass, speed, velocity, momentum, classical kinetic energy, non-relativistic speeds, relativistic speeds, system of particles, work, joules.

This subsection introduces **displacement vector**, **vector sum**, **scalar components** (horizontal and vertical), **unit vector**, and **magnitude** as key quantities for analyzing motion. Students would search for: displacement vector, vector sum, scalar components, horizontal component, vertical component, unit vector, magnitude, direction of a vector, and Cartesian coordinate system. The textbook establishes that a displacement vector equals the vector sum of component displacement vectors (e.g., displacement along stairs plus displacement on hilltop), and that scalar components of displacement depend on step dimensions and number of steps (horizontal component = 200w, vertical component = 200h). It explicitly states that actual distance covered differs from displacement magnitude, and that when an object returns to its initial position, the net displacement vector is zero even though total distance traveled is non-zero. The subsection defines unit vector as a dimensionless quantity found by dividing a vector by its magnitude, and notes that unit vector direction is parallel or antiparallel to coordinate axes when the vector lies along an axis.

This subsection presents a systematic problem-solving procedure for static equilibrium of rigid bodies, introducing the key quantities: forces (with components in x- and y-directions), torques, lever arms, pivot point (rotation axis), and equilibrium conditions. Students would search for: free-body diagram, equilibrium condition, net force, net torque, pivot point, lever arm, rotation axis, and external torques. The textbook establishes that equilibrium requires three conditions—net force in x-direction equals zero, net force in y-direction equals zero, and net torque about the chosen pivot equals zero—and that the number of equations must equal the number of unknowns for solvability. A critical distinction is drawn: free-body diagrams for extended rigid bodies undergoing rotation differ fundamentally from those for translational motion because torque depends on both the acting force and its lever arm, requiring identification of external torques and explicit representation of the body's geometry rather than reduction to a single center-of-mass point. The procedure emphasizes that pivot point selection can be arbitrary but should be chosen to simplify net torque calculations, and that the sign of a solution (positive or negative) determines whether an assumed force direction is correct or opposite to the actual direction.

subsection_title: Kinetic Energy Relative to Different Frames
summary: This subsection introduces **kinetic energy** as a frame-dependent quantity and distinguishes between types of kinetic energy in systems. The key principle is that **kinetic energy of an object can have very different values depending on the frame of reference**, as demonstrated through examples where a person's kinetic energy is calculated relative to the subway car, the tracks, and a frame moving with the person. The textbook establishes that **kinetic energy can never be negative** since it is the product of mass and the square of speed, both always positive or zero. For systems of particles, the subsection identifies distinct types: **translational kinetic energy** (when all particles have the same velocity), **rotational kinetic energy**, **vibrational kinetic energy**, **internal kinetic energy** (relative to an internal frame of reference), and **thermal energy** (associated with random molecular motion). The textbook emphasizes that despite these different names, all forms represent the same physical quantity—energy associated with motion. Search terms: kinetic energy, frame of reference, translational kinetic energy, rotational kinetic energy, vibrational kinetic energy, internal kinetic energy, thermal energy, relative velocity.

This subsection introduces the unit vector of direction, defined as a dimensionless vector obtained by dividing any vector by its magnitude (Equation 2.26). The unit vector is parallel to the original vector and can be expressed in terms of unit vectors of the axes. Key entities include: unit vector, magnitude, velocity vector, dimensionless quantity, and Equation 2.26. The subsection establishes that the unit vector of direction is dimensionless because the numerator and denominator share the same physical unit, and emphasizes computational best practices: carrying calculations to at least three decimal places before rounding to avoid significant numerical errors in final answers.

This subsection demonstrates the application of torque balance to solve static equilibrium problems using a meter stick with attached masses. The key physical quantities and principles introduced are: the first equilibrium condition (sum of forces equals zero), the second equilibrium condition (sum of torques equals zero), lever arms, pivot point selection, and the center of mass location for uniform objects. Students would search for: "torque balance," "static equilibrium conditions," "lever arms," "pivot point," "center of mass of uniform stick," "free-body diagram," and "equilibrium equations." The textbook explicitly states that torque balance depends on identifying lever arms with respect to a chosen pivot, that the center of mass of a uniform stick is located at its midpoint, that torques contributing zero can be omitted from the equilibrium equation, and that the torque balance method is independent of g-values and therefore measures mass (unlike spring balances which measure force). The subsection emphasizes that an appropriate choice of reference frame—such as placing the pivot at the support point—simplifies the solution, even though all inertial frames yield equivalent numerical results.

This subsection introduces three distinct types of kinetic energy: **horizontal kinetic energy** (macroscopic motion of an object relative to its surroundings), **rotational kinetic energy** (from spinning motion), and **internal kinetic energy** or **thermal kinetic energy** (from random molecular motion within an object). The textbook establishes that kinetic energy is calculated from mass and speed using the definition KE = ½mv², and demonstrates this by comparing the horizontal kinetic energy of a basketball in motion to the total translational kinetic energy of air molecules inside it. Key entities and relationships include: kinetic energy depends on mass and speed; thermal kinetic energy arises from average translational kinetic energy of molecules multiplied by the number of molecules; thermal kinetic energy can be orders of magnitude larger than macroscopic kinetic energy; and thermal energy is connected to thermodynamics. Students would search for: "kinetic energy," "horizontal kinetic energy," "rotational kinetic energy," "internal kinetic energy," "thermal kinetic energy," "translational kinetic energy," and "definition of kinetic energy."

This subsection applies static equilibrium to a biomechanics problem involving a weightlifter's forearm holding a 50.0-lb weight, introducing the key quantities: tension in the biceps muscle, force at the elbow joint, weight, lever arms, and torque around the elbow pivot. The textbook identifies three forces acting on the forearm and demonstrates how to construct a free-body diagram with force components (x- and y-components) and apply both the first equilibrium condition (net force equals zero) and the second equilibrium condition (net torque equals zero) to solve for unknown forces. The subsection explicitly states that the x-components of forces parallel to their lever arms do not contribute to torque, that the torque of the force at the elbow is zero because it acts at the pivot, and that contributions to net torque come only from the other forces' y-components. The textbook emphasizes that hinge joints such as the elbow should be assumed to exert force in an arbitrary direction with all components solved independently, and demonstrates that choosing an appropriate reference frame (with axes aligned to the weight direction) can simplify calculations by reducing the number of force components that must be resolved. Key searchable terms: static equilibrium, first equilibrium condition, second equilibrium condition, free-body diagram, torque, lever arm, hinge joint, biceps muscle tension, elbow force.

This subsection introduces two distinct types of vector multiplication used in physics and engineering: the scalar product and the vector product. The scalar product of two vectors yields a scalar (a number) and is used to define work and energy relations, specifically where work is defined as the scalar product of a force vector and a displacement vector. The vector product of two vectors yields a vector and is used to define derived vector quantities such as torque, which is defined as the vector product of an applied force and the distance from pivot to force. The subsection emphasizes that vectors can be multiplied by other vectors but cannot be divided by other vectors, and that distinguishing between scalar products (scalar quantities) and vector products (vector quantities) is essential. Key searchable terms include: scalar product, vector product, work, force, displacement, torque, and vector multiplication.

This subsection introduces the **scalar product** (dot product) of vectors and its computational methods. Key quantities include the **magnitudes of vectors**, the **angle between vectors**, **scalar components** (x-component, y-component), and **unit vectors** (i, j). The textbook establishes that the scalar product can be computed using Equation 2.27 (involving magnitudes and angle) or Equation 2.33 (using scalar components: A·B = A_x B_x + A_y B_y). Critical relationships include: scalar products of orthogonal unit vectors equal zero, scalar products of a unit vector with itself equal one, the scalar product equals the product of one vector's magnitude with the projection of the other vector onto its direction, and the angle between two vectors is found by taking the inverse cosine of (A·B)/(AB). The subsection emphasizes that scalar multiplication is **commutative** and obeys the **distributive law**, and distinguishes the scalar product (a scalar quantity) from the vector product (a vector quantity, exemplified by torque).

The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy; when an object speeds up, net work is positive, and when it slows down, net work is negative. Key quantities include net work, kinetic energy, change in kinetic energy, forces (gravity, normal force), and displacement; students should search for "work-energy theorem," "net work," "change in kinetic energy," "normal force," and "frictionless surface." The theorem establishes that net work depends on all forces acting on an object—omitting or including incorrect forces produces wrong results—and that the normal force does no work because it is perpendicular to displacement. The work-energy theorem simplifies calculations compared to solving Newton's second law, particularly for curved or arbitrary-shaped surfaces where the normal force is non-constant and analytical solutions are difficult or impossible. The problem-solving strategy involves drawing a free-body diagram, determining which forces do work, summing total work, and setting it equal to the change in kinetic energy to solve for unknowns.

This subsection introduces the method for finding the angle between two force vectors using the scalar product (dot product) and vector magnitudes. Key quantities and relationships include: the scalar product (Equation 2.33), the angle formula (Equation 2.34), scalar components of vectors, and vector magnitudes. The textbook establishes that the angle between two vectors is found by dividing the scalar product by the product of the magnitudes and taking the inverse cosine of the result. A student would search for: "angle between two vectors," "scalar product," "dot product," "scalar components," "vector magnitudes," and "Equation 2.33" and "Equation 2.34." The subsection emphasizes that when vectors are expressed in terms of unit vectors along coordinate axes, the angle between them is independent of the specific geographic orientation of those axes (e.g., the angle remains the same whether +x points east or west).

subsection_title: The Vector Product of Two Vectors (the Cross Product)
summary: This subsection introduces the vector product (cross product) of two vectors, denoted A × B, which yields a vector perpendicular to the plane containing both vectors. The magnitude of the vector product is defined as |A × B| = AB sin θ, where θ is the angle measured from the first vector to the second vector (between 0° and 180°). The vector product vanishes when vectors are parallel or antiparallel. The subsection establishes that vector multiplication is anticommutative—reversing the order of multiplication reverses the sign (A × B = −B × A)—and introduces the corkscrew right-hand rule as the standard method for determining the direction of the cross product by rotating a corkscrew handle from the first vector toward the second vector. Search terms: vector product, cross product, magnitude of vector product, anticommutative property, corkscrew right-hand rule, perpendicular to plane, angle between vectors.

subsection_title: A Ladder Resting Against a Wall
summary: This subsection analyzes static equilibrium of a uniform ladder resting against a slippery wall by identifying four forces: normal reaction force N from the floor (vertical), static friction force f along the floor (horizontal), weight w at the center of mass, and normal reaction force F from the wall (horizontal). The textbook establishes equilibrium conditions using a coordinate frame with y-axis vertical and x-axis horizontal, then applies torque analysis with the pivot at the floor contact point, where forces N and f produce zero torque. Key relationships include: the net torque equals the sum of torques from weight and wall reaction (Equation 12.30); the coefficient of static friction is determined when the ladder reaches its minimum inclination angle before slipping; and the result is independent of ladder length because L cancels in the equilibrium condition (Equation 12.31). The subsection emphasizes that torque (the vector product of lever-arm and force vectors) can be computed using Equation 12.10 with the angle measured counterclockwise from lever arm to force direction, and that the ladder will slip when net torque becomes negative if static friction is insufficient. Search terms: static equilibrium, ladder, normal reaction force, static friction force, weight, torque, lever arm, pivot point, coefficient of static friction, inclination angle, slippery wall.

This subsection applies the work-energy theorem to determine stopping forces in bullet penetration problems. Key quantities introduced are initial kinetic energy, average stopping force, stopping distance (penetration depth), and change in kinetic energy. The work-energy theorem states that initial kinetic energy equals the average stopping force times the distance penetrated; equivalently, the change in kinetic energy equals the net work done. The subsection demonstrates that when a bullet loses all its kinetic energy penetrating boards, both the change in kinetic energy and net work done are negative. A concrete example calculates the average stopping force (~7.6 × 10⁴ N) for a 2.60 g bullet with muzzle velocity 335 m/s penetrating eight pine boards over a total distance of 0.152 m. The subsection also establishes that penetration distance depends on the change in kinetic energy: when a bullet hits off-center and the block rotates, the bullet retains some kinetic energy, resulting in smaller penetration than when fired dead center and losing all kinetic energy.

This subsection applies static equilibrium principles to analyze forces on door hinges supporting a swinging door with uniform mass density. The key quantities are the unknown force components at hinges A and B, the known weight acting at the center of mass (located at the geometrical center due to uniform density), and the hinge separation distance. The subsection establishes that four independent equilibrium equations are required to solve for the four unknown component forces: equilibrium conditions for forces in the x-direction, forces in the y-direction, torques about a pivot point (the upper hinge), and the constraint that weight is evenly distributed between hinges. The forces exerted by the door on its hinges are found using Newton's third law by reversing the hinge forces on the door. The subsection emphasizes that the assumption of symmetric weight distribution between hinges is essential—without it, the number of unknowns would exceed the number of equilibrium equations, making the problem unsolvable.

This subsection introduces **power** as the relationship between work done and the time interval required to do it. Key quantities include **average power** (work divided by time interval), **instantaneous power** (power at a specific moment), and **work**, which connects to power through the relationships: when power is constant, average power equals instantaneous power and work equals power times time interval; when power varies with time, work equals the time integral of power. The subsection establishes that **power is the rate of transfer of energy** and relates power to the **work-energy theorem**. Power is measured in **watts** (joules per second) in SI units, with **horsepower** as an alternative unit for everyday devices. Students would search for: power, average power, instantaneous power, work-energy theorem, rate of energy transfer, watts, horsepower.

This subsection introduces **torque** (τ) as the vector product τ = **R** × **F**, where **R** is the radial vector from the pivot (nut) to the point of force application and **F** is the applied force vector. The magnitude and direction of torque depend on the magnitude of the force, its direction relative to the lever arm, and the distance from the pivot; torque is largest when the force is perpendicular to the lever arm (sin(θ) = 1), giving maximum mechanical advantage. The direction of torque is determined using the **corkscrew right-hand rule**, with the torque vector lying along the z-axis perpendicular to the xy-plane containing **R** and **F**. The subsection establishes that the **cross product** is **anticommutative** and **distributive**, and provides rules for cross products of unit vectors: unit vectors in **cyclic order** (**i** × **j** = **k**, **j** × **k** = **i**, **k** × **i** = **j**) yield the remaining unit vector, while non-cyclic order yields the antiparallel unit vector. Students can compute cross products using either **Equation 2.35** (magnitude-direction form) or **Equation 2.40** (component form), with angles measured counterclockwise from the first vector to the second vector.

This subsection introduces **power** as the rate of doing work, defined as the limit of average power as time intervals approach zero. Key quantities include **work**, **force**, **displacement**, **velocity**, and **time**, with power measured in **watts** (joules per second) or **horsepower**. The textbook establishes that power expended by a force is related to both the work done against gravity over a distance and the product of force and velocity. A concrete example demonstrates these principles through an 80-kg army trainee performing pull-ups: raising the body (excluding 10% arm mass) in 0.8 seconds against gravitational force, yielding power expenditure of somewhat more than one horsepower. The subsection connects force, displacement, and velocity through the relationship that power depends on the forces acting on a body and the velocity of that body during motion.

subsection_title: Tensile or Compressive Stress, Strain, and Young’s Modulus
summary: This subsection introduces tensile and compressive stress and strain, which occur when antiparallel forces of equal magnitude act perpendicular to an object's cross-section, causing elongation (positive length change) or contraction (negative length change). Stress is defined as the ratio of deforming force to cross-sectional area A, while strain is the fractional change in length; forces parallel to the cross-section do not change object length. Tensile stress and strain describe stretching deformation, whereas compressive stress and strain describe contracting deformation, with compressive values calculated using absolute values. Young's modulus Y is the elastic modulus that relates stress to strain for both tensile and compressive deformation, defined by Equation 12.33. Key searchable entities include: tensile stress, compressive stress, tensile strain, compressive strain, Young's modulus, elastic modulus, deforming force, cross-sectional area, elongation, and contraction.

This subsection introduces **stress** and **strain** as the two fundamental quantities describing deformation, and **elastic modulus** as the proportionality constant relating them in the linear limit. Stress is defined as force per unit area (measured in pascals, psi, or atm) and encompasses **tensile stress** (pulling/elongation), **compressive stress** (compression), **bulk stress** (all-sided squeezing), and **shear stress** (tangential forces); strain is a dimensionless fractional change in length, volume, or geometry corresponding to each stress type. The textbook states that at sufficiently low stress values, stress and strain are directly proportional according to the relation stress = elastic modulus × strain, where the elastic modulus has the same units as stress. Three specific elastic moduli are defined: **Young's modulus** (for tensile stress), **bulk modulus** (for bulk stress), and **shear modulus** (for shear stress); materials with large elastic moduli show small deformation under stress, while small elastic moduli produce large strain. The subsection emphasizes that the stress-strain relationship is an observed, laboratory-measured relation and provides a reference table of elastic moduli values for various materials under different physical conditions. Students would search for: deformation, stress, strain, elastic modulus, tensile stress, compressive stress, bulk stress, shear stress, Young's modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus, linear limit.

chapter_title: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy
section_title: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy
subsection_title: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy
summary: This subsection introduces the principle of conservation of energy and the concept of potential energy as fundamental tools for analyzing energy changes in physical systems. Key quantities and principles include: conservation of energy, potential energy, kinetic energy, conservation of mechanical energy, and energy transfers. The subsection establishes that conservation of energy governs changes in kinetic energy and relates them to changes in other forms of energy associated with a system's interactions. Potential energy enables formulation of the law of conservation of mechanical energy, which applies to simple systems. The law of conservation of energy is presented as a fundamental principle that extends to increasingly complex systems and varied forms of energy. Search terms: potential energy, conservation of energy, kinetic energy, conservation of mechanical energy, energy transfers, law of conservation of energy.

subsection_title: A Particle in a Magnetic Field
summary: This subsection introduces the magnetic force on a charged particle moving through a magnetic field, establishing that the magnetic force vector is proportional to the vector product (cross product) of the velocity vector and the magnetic field vector. Key quantities include the magnetic field vector, velocity vector, magnetic force vector, and the angle between the force and field vectors. Students would search for: magnetic force, vector product, cross product, scalar product, dot product, velocity vector, magnetic field vector, magnitude of magnetic force, and direction angle. The subsection explicitly states that the magnetic force vector is perpendicular to both the velocity vector and the magnetic field vector as a consequence of the vector product definition, and that the scalar product (dot product) of the magnetic force and magnetic field equals zero. The text distinguishes between the dot product (which yields a scalar) and the cross product (which yields a vector), noting these terms are used interchangeably with scalar product and vector product respectively. Methods for computing the magnetic force include using components (Equation 2.41) or computing the magnitude directly (Equation 2.35), with direction angles found via scalar product and Equation 2.34.

This subsection introduces **kinematics**, the discipline that describes motion through the properties of **position**, **time**, **velocity**, and **acceleration**, distinct from **dynamics**, which concerns the causes of motion. Key entities include: **kinematics**, **dynamics**, **position**, **displacement** (changes in position), **velocity**, **acceleration** (changes in velocity), **one-dimensional motion**, and **multidimensional motion**. The textbook establishes that kinematics can fully describe motion—including calculating **displacements**, **velocities**, and **accelerations**—without reference to an object's **mass** or the **forces** involved. One-dimensional motion is presented as foundational; the tools developed for one-dimensional motion provide the basis necessary to study motion in two and three dimensions. The maglev train example illustrates how an object in one-dimensional motion has different positions at various times, resulting in displacements and changes in velocity that can be analyzed kinematically.

This subsection introduces **compressive stress**, **compressive strain**, and **Young's modulus** in the context of a loaded vertical pillar. Key entities include: stress (σ = N/A), strain (ε = σ/Y), Young's modulus (Y), normal force (N), cross-sectional area (A), and material density. The textbook establishes that normal force on a pillar's cross-section equals the sum of the sculpture's weight and the weight of the pillar segment above that cross-section, and that compressive strain is calculated by dividing compressive stress by Young's modulus. A critical relationship stated is that normal force varies along the pillar's length—smallest at the top and largest at the base—which means compressive stress is largest at the pillar's base when cross-sectional area is uniform. The example uses granite (density 2,700 kg/m³, Young's modulus 4.5 × 10¹⁰ Pa) supporting a 10,000 N sculpture on a 6.0-m-tall pillar.

chapter_title: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy
summary: This subsection introduces **gravitational potential energy**, **kinetic energy**, **potential energy difference**, and the relationship between work and potential energy in a system. Key entities include: potential energy of a system, gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, work done by gravitational force, potential energy difference, and reference point (or zero potential energy). The textbook establishes that as a projectile rises, negative work by gravity decreases kinetic energy while increasing gravitational potential energy of the football-Earth system; conversely, as it falls, positive work increases kinetic energy as gravitational potential energy decreases. Potential energy difference from point A to point B is defined as the negative of the work done, and absolute potential energy values require an arbitrary reference point chosen for convenience (commonly the lowest height or farthest distance in a problem). The subsection states that change in kinetic energy equals the negative of change in gravitational potential energy when friction and air resistance are absent, a relationship generalizable to any potential energy.

This subsection introduces **tensile stress**, **tensile strain**, **elongation**, and **Young's modulus** as key quantities for analyzing elastic deformation in loaded rods. Students would search for: "tensile stress," "Young's modulus," "elongation," "Equation 12.34," "Equation 12.36," "compressive stress," "I-beams," and "elastic modulus." The textbook establishes that tensile stress in a vertical rod is computed using Equation 12.34, elongation is found by inverting Equation 12.36, and Young's modulus (from Table 12.1) connects stress and strain in the calculation. Stress distribution is non-uniform along a rod's length when the rod's weight is considered—largest at the top and smallest at the bottom. Objects frequently experience both compressive stress and tensile stress simultaneously, exemplified by loaded shelves and beams that sag: the top surface experiences compressive stress while the bottom surface experiences tensile stress. Modern I-beams reduce bending strains in construction, and the compression or tension in supporting columns changes when loads shift position.

This subsection introduces the foundational kinematic quantities **position (x)**, **displacement (Δx)**, and **frame of reference** needed to describe one-dimensional motion. **Position** is the location of an object at a particular time specified relative to a **frame of reference**—an arbitrary set of axes that can be stationary (e.g., Earth) or in motion (e.g., an airplane). **Displacement** is defined as the change in position (final position minus initial position) and is a vector quantity that can be positive or negative depending on the choice of positive direction; it is calculated using the delta notation Δx. The subsection distinguishes **displacement** from **distance traveled**: displacement is the change in position (sum of individual displacements), while distance traveled is the total length of the path; correspondingly, **magnitude of displacement** (always positive, the absolute value) differs from distance traveled. Key search terms: position, displacement, frame of reference, Δx, distance traveled, magnitude of displacement, vector, one-dimensional motion.

chapter_title: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy
summary: This subsection introduces the fundamental relationship between potential energy and work: the difference in potential energy equals the negative of the work done by a force. Key quantities include potential energy (U), work (W), force (F), and displacement along the x-axis; the subsection emphasizes that work is the dot product of force with distance, which simplifies to multiplication in one-dimensional motion. The textbook establishes that potential energy functions are obtained through integration of force functions, with the constant of integration determined by boundary conditions at a chosen zero point. A central principle presented is that conservative forces—those whose work is independent of path and can be integrated—have associated potential energy functions; the potential energy difference between two points always equals the negative work done by the conservative force between those points. The subsection demonstrates this relationship through the example of a linear restoring force F(x) = −kx and shows how to calculate both potential energy differences and absolute potential energy values at specific positions by substituting x-values into the derived potential energy function.

This subsection introduces bulk stress (pressure), bulk strain (volume change), and their relationship through the bulk modulus. Key entities include: pressure (p), defined as force normal to a surface divided by unit surface area (A); bulk stress, the increase in pressure over atmospheric reference level; bulk strain, described as change in volume relative to original volume; bulk modulus (B), the proportionality constant relating bulk stress to bulk strain (Equation 12.33); and compressibility, the reciprocal of bulk modulus used for fluids. The textbook establishes that pressure is a scalar quantity acting equally in all directions, that an increase in bulk stress causes an increase in bulk strain, and that an increase in pressure (positive) always causes a decrease in volume (negative), necessitating a minus sign in the bulk modulus equation (Equation 12.39). Compressibility describes the change in volume of a fluid per unit increase in pressure, with fluids of large compressibility being relatively easy to compress.

This subsection introduces shear stress, shear strain, and shear modulus as properties of solid objects (such as buildings and tectonic plates) that do not apply to fluids. Shear deformation occurs when two antiparallel forces of equal magnitude are applied tangentially to opposite surfaces of a solid, causing a gradual shift of layers tangent to the acting forces. Shear strain is defined as the ratio of the largest displacement to the transverse distance, and shear strain is caused by shear stress. Shear stress is measured as the magnitude of the shearing force per surface area A. The shear modulus (denoted S) is the proportionality constant defined by the ratio of shear stress to shear strain. Key searchable entities: shear stress, shear strain, shear modulus, shear deformation, solid objects, antiparallel forces, transverse direction, displacement, surface area.

chapter_title: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy
summary: This subsection introduces the concept that each type of interaction in a system corresponds to a type of potential energy, with total potential energy defined as the sum of all individual potential energy types—a relationship following from the additive property of the dot product in work expressions. For a system consisting of Earth and particles (or bodies) near its surface, the gravitational force on each particle equals its weight mg acting vertically downward. The work done by Earth's uniform gravitational force depends on the mass of the body, the acceleration due to gravity g, and the difference in height traversed; this work equals the negative of the change in gravitational potential energy. The gravitational potential energy function near Earth's surface is given by U(y) = mgy, where the constant can be chosen arbitrarily but is conventionally set to zero at the lowest vertical position in the problem. Students searching for this content should look for: potential energy of a system, types of potential energy, gravitational potential energy, gravitational potential energy function, weight mg, uniform gravitational force, work done by gravitational force, and U(y) = mgy.

This subsection introduces **position**, **displacement**, **distance traveled**, **average velocity**, and **elapsed time** through a multi-leg trip example. Key entities students would search for include: position, displacement, average velocity, distance traveled, magnitude of displacement, and elapsed time. The textbook establishes that **average velocity is calculated from positions at two different times** (x₁ at t₁ and x₂ at t₂), and that **displacement and elapsed time can be calculated from position and time data given in a problem**. The subsection explicitly states that **total displacement is the sum of individual displacements**, **magnitude of total displacement is the absolute value of total displacement**, and **total distance traveled is the sum of magnitudes of individual displacements**. It demonstrates that **if an object ends at its starting position, total displacement and average velocity are both zero**, and that **position versus time can be graphed as a useful aid to visualize motion**. The concrete example shows Jill's total displacement of −0.75 km (meaning she ends due west of her home) and total distance traveled of 3.75 km over 58 minutes of elapsed time.

This subsection introduces **instantaneous velocity** (also called simply velocity), defined as the limit of average velocity as the time interval and displacement between two points approach zero. The key relationship is that instantaneous velocity equals the rate of change of the position function x(t), which geometrically corresponds to the slope of the position graph at a specific time point. Instantaneous velocity is a vector quantity with dimensions of length per time. The subsection establishes that when the slope of the position graph is zero—occurring at maxima and minima of the position function—the instantaneous velocity is zero; conversely, zeros of the velocity function identify the minimum and maximum points of the position function. Students searching for this content should look for: **instantaneous velocity**, **velocity**, **average velocity**, **position function x(t)**, **rate of change**, **slope of position graph**, **limit as time interval approaches zero**, and **maxima and minima of position**.

This subsection introduces **shear modulus**, **shear stress**, and **shear strain** through a worked example of a bookcase deformed by a tangential force. A 50.0-N horizontal push on the top shelf of a 180.0 cm tall, 90.0 cm wide bookcase causes a 15.0 cm displacement relative to the stationary bottom shelf; the shear modulus can be calculated from the physical dimensions, tangential force, and resulting displacement. The textbook establishes that shear deformation depends on tangential force and the geometry of the object, and that excessive shear stress can cause structural failure—a mechanism the text explicitly connects to real-world phenomena including collapse of earth-filled dams, levees, and landslides. The subsection also notes that Young's modulus and shear modulus do not apply to fluids. **Search terms:** shear modulus, shear stress, shear strain, tangential force, elastic modulus, static equilibrium, elasticity, structural failure.

chapter_title: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy
subsection_title: Gravitational Potential Energy of a Hiker
summary: This subsection introduces **gravitational potential energy** of a hiker-Earth system and demonstrates how to calculate it using a reference height. Key quantities include the **hiker's mass** (75 kg), **height differences** (147 m above base, 195 m below sea level), and **gravitational potential energy values** (approximately 1.08 × 10⁵ J at summit, −1.43 × 10⁵ J at sea level, relative to base). The textbook establishes that **gravitational potential energy depends on the choice of zero potential energy** (origin of the y-axis), but **differences in potential energy are independent of this choice** and thus physically meaningful. Students searching for this content would look for: **gravitational potential energy**, **potential energy of a system**, **choice of zero potential energy**, **reference height**, **Equation 8.5**, and **hiker-Earth system**. The subsection also connects this concept to **elastic potential energy** and **spring force**, noting that the **difference of elastic potential energy equals the negative of work done by the spring force**, and that the **zero of potential energy is most conveniently placed at the unstretched length of the spring** when spring force is the only force acting.

subsection_title: Finding Velocity from a Position-Versus-Time Graph
summary: This subsection introduces **instantaneous velocity**, defined as the limit of average velocity as elapsed time approaches zero, or equivalently as the derivative of position (x) with respect to time (t). Students can find instantaneous velocity from a **position-versus-time graph** by determining the **slope** of the curve at any point; a positive slope indicates motion away from the origin with positive velocity, zero slope indicates no position change, and negative slope indicates motion back toward the origin with negative velocity. The subsection distinguishes **velocity** (a vector with direction) from **speed** (a scalar with no direction), establishing that **average speed** equals total distance divided by elapsed time, while **average velocity** equals total displacement divided by elapsed time—these are not equivalent when a trip returns to its starting point. **Instantaneous speed** is calculated from the magnitude of instantaneous velocity; particles with velocities of +7.0 m/s and −7.0 m/s have different velocities but identical speeds of 7.0 m/s. This subsection examines how Earth's rotation affects gravitational measurements at different latitudes away from the equator. The key quantities are centripetal acceleration, effective gravity (apparent weight), and the radius of Earth, which varies by approximately 30 km between the equator and poles. The textbook establishes that at the poles, centripetal acceleration is zero and apparent weight equals true weight, while at other latitudes, centripetal acceleration (directed toward the rotation axis) combines vectorially with weight such that effective gravity no longer points toward Earth's center. This deviation causes plumb bobs and buildings to align along the deviated direction rather than along a radius through Earth's center, producing deviations of several feet in the tallest structures. The subsection states that the rotation effect produces a 0.34% correction to gravity at the equator, and that Earth's oblate shape (bulging at the equator due to rotation and partial liquid interior) contributes a comparable difference in the same direction, together explaining why apparent weight decreases toward the tropics. subsection_title: How Far Does a Car Go?
summary: This subsection applies kinematic equations for motion with constant acceleration to calculate stopping distances for a car under different surface conditions. Key quantities include initial velocity (v₀ = 30.0 m/s), final velocity (v = 0), acceleration (a = −7.00 m/s² on dry concrete, −5.00 m/s² on wet concrete), displacement (x − x₀), and reaction time (0.500 s). The subsection demonstrates that displacement depends on acceleration—stopping distance is shorter on dry concrete (64.3 m) than wet concrete (90.0 m)—and that reaction time adds significantly to total displacement (15.0 m in this example). The problem-solving approach emphasizes identifying knowns and unknowns, selecting kinematic equations with only one unknown variable when possible, and recognizing that during reaction time, velocity remains constant while the car continues to travel before braking begins. Students searching for content on stopping distance, braking distance, reaction time effects, or kinematic equations applied to real-world scenarios would find this subsection relevant.

chapter_title: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy
summary: This subsection introduces major forms of energy and their transformations: thermal energy (internal kinetic energy of atoms and molecules related to temperature), chemical energy (potential energy in molecular structure of fuels), electrical energy, radiant energy (electromagnetic radiation including visible light, infrared, radio, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays), nuclear energy (from mass-energy conversion in nuclear reactions), and mechanical energy. Key principles include the law of conservation of energy (total energy in an isolated system remains constant) and energy conservation (philosophy of reducing energy use through efficiency). The textbook establishes that energy transforms continuously between forms—chemical energy converts to thermal energy through oxidation or metabolism, radiant energy converts to chemical energy through photosynthesis, thermal energy converts to mechanical energy via turbines, and radiant energy converts to electricity through the photoelectric effect in photovoltaics. Energy sources divide into renewable sources (replenished on timescales shorter than civilization's lifetime: hydropower, wind power, geothermal power, solar power, biomass) and non-renewable sources (depleted once extracted: fossil fuels accounting for ~81% of world consumption, nuclear energy at ~3%), with the critical distinction that most energy transformations ultimately produce waste heat, degrading useful work despite energy conservation.

section_title: Gravitational Potential Energy and Total Energy
summary: This subsection introduces gravitational potential energy for large distances where g varies significantly, deriving it from first principles using work and the definition of potential energy. Key quantities include work (W), gravitational potential energy (U), gravitational force, mass (m), and distance from Earth's center; the subsection establishes that potential energy is defined as the negative of work done by the gravitational force. The textbook states that gravitational force is a conservative force (magnitude and direction depend on location only), enabling path-independent work calculations, and derives the expression for U by decomposing motion into radial and arc segments. Critical relationships include: U approaches zero as distance approaches infinity (the reference point for zero potential energy); U becomes increasingly negative as masses get closer; positive work against gravity increases U (makes it less negative); and all masses naturally fall from higher to lower potential energy. Students would search for: gravitational potential energy, conservative force, work-energy relationships, potential energy reference point, and gravitational force over large distances.

This subsection introduces the law of gravitation for spherically symmetrical objects and the gravitational acceleration g at various distances from Earth's surface and interior. Key quantities and relationships include: Equation 13.1 and Equation 13.2 (valid only for r ≥ R, the body's radius); g = 8.7 m/s² at 400 km altitude where the International Space Station orbits; and Gauss's law applied to gravitation, which establishes that only mass within radius r contributes to gravitational force, with that mass acting as if located at the center. For a spherical planet with constant density, g decreases linearly with descent toward the center, where gravitational acceleration becomes zero and an object is weightless due to equal pulls in all directions. The subsection contrasts the theoretical g-profile for constant-density Earth with the actual profile derived from seismic data, and explores a spherical shell planet scenario where g at the surface matches Earth's but becomes zero in the interior, eliminating gravitational effects for travel between surface points. Search terms: law of gravitation, spherically symmetrical objects, gravitational acceleration, Gauss's law, mass within r, constant density planet, spherical shell planet, weightlessness at center.

This subsection teaches how to solve for time t in constant acceleration problems by selecting kinematic equations with a single unknown. Key quantities include displacement (x), initial velocity (v₀), acceleration (a), and time (t); the subsection emphasizes using the kinematic equation that contains only the unknown variable t to avoid unnecessary complexity. When kinematic equations contain an unknown squared, the quadratic formula yields two mathematical solutions; however, only one solution is typically physically reasonable—negative time values are rejected because they would imply motion occurred before the event began. The subsection demonstrates this principle through a worked example of a car merging onto a freeway ramp (x = 200 m, v₀ = 10.0 m/s, a = 2.00 m/s²), which produces solutions t = 10.0 s and t = −20.0 s, with only the positive value accepted. Students searching for content on solving for time in constant acceleration, using kinematic equations to find unknown variables, or interpreting multiple solutions from quadratic equations will find this material relevant.

This subsection introduces **linear momentum** as a conserved quantity in closed systems, analogous to energy conservation. It presents the **impulse-momentum theorem** as a fundamental relationship that constrains how physical systems evolve over time. The subsection establishes that conservation of momentum is particularly useful for analyzing **collisions** and provides an alternative to Newton's laws for studying complex systems with nonconstant forces. Key search terms: linear momentum, conservation of momentum, impulse-momentum theorem, collisions, conserved quantity, closed system. The text explicitly states that momentum conservation, like energy conservation, restricts the possible ways a system can change—systems cannot evolve randomly but must obey momentum conservation principles.

Linear momentum (p) is a vector quantity defined as the product of an object's mass and velocity (p = mv), characterizing the "quantity of motion" of an object. Unlike kinetic energy, momentum depends equally on mass and velocity, making it distinct from kinetic energy and useful for determining whether an object's motion is difficult or easy to change over a short time interval. The textbook illustrates momentum's dependence on both mass and velocity through contrasting examples: an air molecule at room temperature (mass 4.8 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, speed 500 m/s, momentum 2.4 × 10⁻²³ kg·m/s) and an automobile (mass 1400 kg, speed 15 m/s, momentum 2.1 × 10⁴ kg·m/s), which differ by 27 orders of magnitude. Momentum is particularly useful in analyzing collisions and predicting resistance to changes in motion. Search terms: momentum, linear momentum, p = mv, vector quantity, mass, velocity, kinetic energy, collisions.

Key relationships include: escape velocity depends on the mass M and radius R of the astronomical body; the object's kinetic energy at the surface converts entirely to gravitational potential energy as it reaches infinity; and escape velocity is independent of the object's mass m, applying equally to all objects regardless of their mass. This subsection introduces **impulse** as the product of force and time interval, defined mathematically as J = ∫F(t)dt for time-dependent forces and J = F·Δt for constant forces. Key relationships stated include: impulse equals average force multiplied by time interval (J = <F>(t₂−t₁)), and impulse can be determined by measurement or calculation even without knowing the detailed force function F(t)—only the average force is needed. The subsection emphasizes that the process is "usually reversed": impulse is determined first, then used to calculate the average force that produced it. section_title: Gravitational Potential Energy and Total Energy
summary: This subsection introduces **escape velocity** and **escape speed** as the initial velocity (or speed at any position) required for an object to escape a celestial body, defined more generally as the speed at which total energy equals zero. The textbook establishes that **total energy** determines whether an object escapes: if total energy is zero or greater, the object escapes and is **not gravitationally bound**; if total energy is negative, the object cannot escape and is **gravitationally bound to** the massive body. Specific escape speeds are provided: approximately 11 km/s from Earth's surface and 42 km/s from the Sun (starting from Earth's orbit). The subsection explains that escape velocity is independent of the escaping object's mass and describes practical methods to reduce required velocity, including Earth's rotational velocity (460 m/s at the equator), Earth's orbital velocity around the Sun (30 km/s), and **gravitational assist** or **gravity slingshot technique** using planetary encounters. The textbook notes that **Equation 13.5** and **Equation 13.6** apply to point objects and spherically symmetric objects (provided r exceeds the sum of radii), and that energy conservation is a scalar equation where velocity direction plays no role.

This subsection introduces **two-body pursuit problems** involving motion with constant acceleration, where two objects in motion are linked by a common parameter. This subsection applies impulse-momentum theorem and Newton's third law to estimate forces during the Arizona Meteor Crater impact event. Key quantities introduced are impulse, average force, maximum force, momentum change, and impact duration; the subsection establishes that average force relates to impulse by F_avg = Δp/Δt, and that mass equals density times volume (m = ρV). The textbook demonstrates calculating the meteor's mass from its density (8000 kg/m³), spherical volume, impact velocity (12.8 km/s), and impact duration (~130 s) to obtain average force (~2.55 × 10¹⁵ N). A time-dependent force function F(t) is chosen to model the impact, with maximum force at contact that rapidly decreases to zero; the integral of this force function equals the impulse, and graphically the area under F(t) represents impulse. The subsection applies Newton's third law to relate the force Earth exerts on the meteor to the force the meteor exerts on Earth, and notes that despite the enormous impact force, Earth's resulting acceleration was immeasurable, though the impact generated detectable seismic waves.

Free fall describes one-dimensional motion of an object falling in a gravitational field near Earth or other celestial bodies, where air resistance and friction are negligible. The key principle is that all objects fall with the same constant acceleration due to gravity (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²) independent of mass, a fact experimentally established by Galileo. Acceleration due to gravity is caused by the force of gravity pulling objects toward Earth's center, and its constant value allows kinematic equations to apply to falling objects. The magnitude g varies slightly (9.78–9.83 m/s²) with latitude, altitude, and local geology, but a standard value of 9.8 m/s² is used. In coordinate systems, acceleration a equals −g when upward is positive and +g when downward is positive. Air resistance and friction oppose motion and cause real-world deviations from ideal free fall, such as lighter objects falling slower than heavier ones of the same size.

This subsection introduces circular orbits of satellites and derives the key relationships governing orbital motion. The primary physical quantities are **orbital speed**, **orbital period**, **escape velocity**, **centripetal acceleration**, and **total energy**; the subsection establishes that orbital speed and escape velocity depend only on distance from the planet's center, not on the satellite's mass. The textbook states that **Newton's second law** combined with **gravitational force** yields orbital speed, that **escape velocity is approximately 40% greater than orbital velocity** at any radius, and that **orbital period increases with distance from the Sun** (confirming Copernicus's observation and representing **Kepler's third law** for circular orbits). An object with **negative total energy** is **gravitationally bound** and therefore in orbit. The subsection explains that astronauts in orbit experience **weightlessness** because they are in **free fall**, with Earth's surface curving away at the same rate they fall toward it—the defining condition of a circular orbit. Search terms: circular orbits, orbital speed, orbital period, escape velocity, centripetal acceleration, gravitationally bound, Kepler's third law, free fall, orbital velocity, total energy.

This subsection introduces **impulse** (J), **change in momentum** (Δp), and **average force** as related quantities in collision analysis, establishing that impulse equals change in momentum (J = Δp). The textbook demonstrates how **collision time** directly affects the **average force** experienced by a driver: extending collision time from 0.20 s to 2.5 s reduces average force from approximately 14 times the driver's weight to 1.1 times his weight, even though the **change of momentum** remains identical. Key entities include: impulse, momentum, average force, collision time, velocity, mass, and weight. This subsection introduces orbital speed and orbital period as key quantities determined by Equation 13.7 and Equation 13.8, respectively, for satellites orbiting above Earth's surface where orbital radius equals Earth's radius plus orbital altitude. The ISS exemplifies low Earth orbit (LEO) with an orbital velocity of about 17,000 mph and period of just over 90 minutes; other LEO examples include weather satellites, while GPS satellites at about 20,000 km represent medium Earth orbit. The subsection establishes that higher orbits require more energy both to place satellites there and to reach them for repairs. Geosynchronous orbit satellites are positioned at a specific distance just above the equator such that their orbital period is 1 day, causing them to remain in a fixed position relative to Earth's surface; these satellites are used for fixed satellite dishes like TV reception dishes. Search terms: orbital speed, orbital period, low Earth orbit (LEO), medium Earth orbit, geosynchronous orbit, ISS, GPS satellites, orbital altitude, orbital radius, orbital velocity.

This subsection introduces one-dimensional motion under gravity with constant acceleration of magnitude g, analyzing straight up-and-down motion with no air resistance or friction. Key entities include: free fall (motion after an object leaves contact with a supporting surface), vertical displacement (represented by y), initial velocity, and the kinematic equations (Equation 3.15 through Equation 3.17). The textbook establishes that acceleration g is negative when the positive direction is defined as upward, and positive when the positive direction is defined as downward; the sign of acceleration depends on the chosen coordinate system. An object is in free fall only while airborne—once it contacts the ground or another object, the constant acceleration g no longer applies. The subsection emphasizes a problem-solving strategy: define the coordinate system to determine the sign of g, record knowns and unknowns, then select the appropriate kinematic equations to solve for unknowns.

This subsection introduces the **impulse-momentum theorem**, which states that an impulse applied to a system equals the change in the system's momentum (Δp = FΔt). Key quantities include **impulse** (force acting over a time interval), **momentum**, **force**, **velocity**, and **time interval**. The subsection emphasizes that impulse is a **vector quantity**, meaning direction matters—impulses in opposite directions cause opposite changes in momentum. An impulse causes a **change in momentum**, not momentum itself; calculating this change requires subtracting initial momentum from final momentum and carefully accounting for vector signs. Common problem types involve calculating the **applied force** or **change of velocity** resulting from an impulse, solved by expressing impulse both as force times time interval and as change of momentum, then equating these expressions. The subsection illustrates that the same change in momentum can result from different force-time combinations (e.g., airbags reduce force by extending the time interval).

This subsection introduces **free fall**, **kinematic equations**, **acceleration** (−g), **position**, **velocity**, and **coordinate systems** for analyzing the motion of a falling ball. Key search terms include: free fall, kinematic equations, acceleration equals −g, initial velocity, position, velocity, quadratic equation, coordinate system, positive direction upward, negative direction downward, and physical significance of roots. The textbook establishes that in free fall, acceleration equals −g with the positive direction upward; it demonstrates how to apply kinematic equations (Equation 3.16 and Equation 3.15) by substituting given values to obtain a quadratic equation whose roots must be evaluated for physical meaning. The subsection explicitly states that the positive root represents the physically meaningful time when the ball was released, while the negative root represents a time before release and is not physically meaningful. This subsection applies the impulse-momentum theorem to calculate the average force exerted by the Enterprise's impulse engines during acceleration. The key relationship is the scalar form of the impulse-momentum theorem: F·Δt = m·Δv, which connects force, time interval, mass, and change in velocity. The subsection demonstrates how knowing initial velocity, final velocity, time interval, and mass allows calculation of average force using F = m(v_f - v_i)/Δt, and subsequently acceleration using Newton's Second Law (a = F/m). This subsection demonstrates how to determine the mass of Earth using the Moon's orbital data and Equation 13.8, which relates orbital period and radius to the central body's mass. Key quantities include the Moon's orbital period (27.3 days), the average Earth-Moon distance (384,000 km), and the resulting calculated mass of Earth, which can be compared to values obtained from surface gravitational acceleration (g). The textbook establishes that the two methods yield results within ~0.8% agreement, though both rely on average values; it notes that g varies ~0.5% from equator to poles, while the Moon's elliptical orbit causes orbital radius r to vary over 10%. The subsection emphasizes that objects moving upward away from Earth are also in a state of free fall, and that the entire upward-and-downward motion can be analyzed using a single equation rather than breaking it into two segments.

This subsection applies the impulse-momentum relationship to analyze forces during a collision by examining an iPhone dropped from chest height. Key quantities introduced are impulse, momentum, change in momentum, average force, collision time, and impact velocity; the textbook establishes that impulse equals change in momentum (J = Δp) and that average force relates to impulse divided by collision time (F_avg = J/Δt). This subsection introduces the relationship between average force, momentum change, and time interval: average force equals the change in momentum divided by the time interval over which the change occurs. The textbook establishes that for continuously changing momentum due to continuously changing force, the rate of change of the system's momentum equals the net applied force—Newton's second law expressed in terms of momentum rather than acceleration. The subsection emphasizes that this momentum-force relationship is Newton's original formulation from Principia Mathematica (where he used the term "quantity of motion"). When mass remains constant, the momentum-force equation reduces to the familiar F = ma form; however, a key advantage of the momentum formulation is that it remains valid even when the mass of the system is not constant, allowing both mass and velocity to change. The textbook identifies applications including car crashes, punting a football, and collisions of subatomic particles, where collision times are small but measurable (typically 1/10th to 1/1000th of a second). This subsection applies Newton's law of universal gravitation and Newton's second law to determine the orbital velocity and period of two galaxies in circular orbit about their common center of mass. Key quantities introduced are orbital velocity (tangential speed), orbital period, centripetal acceleration, and the radius of orbit, which for equal-mass objects equals half the separation distance between their centers. The textbook establishes that Equations 13.7 and 13.8 cannot be used directly because they assume one mass orbits a much larger central mass, whereas here two equal masses orbit their mutual center of mass. For the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies (each 800 billion solar masses, separated by 2.5 million light-years), the subsection demonstrates that orbital velocity is determined from centripetal acceleration, orbital period is calculated from orbital velocity, and the resulting orbital period of approximately 50 billion years is nearly four times the age of the Universe. summary: This subsection introduces the foundational concepts for analyzing motion in two and three dimensions, establishing that most objects follow curved trajectories rather than straight-line paths. The key physical quantities—position vector, displacement, velocity, and acceleration—are extended from one-dimensional motion to two and three dimensions, with the critical modification that these quantities must be treated as vectors. Students searching for content on position vectors, velocity vectors, acceleration vectors, curved trajectories, projectile motion, circular motion, and relative motion will find this material.

This subsection introduces **linear momentum** (the product of mass and velocity) and the **conservation of linear momentum** principle. Key entities include: momentum, mass, velocity, change in velocity (dv), time interval (dt), rate of change of momentum, force, and collision/interaction. The textbook establishes that during an interaction between two objects, although individual masses and velocity changes differ, the products of mass and velocity change are equal in magnitude; consequently, the rate of change of momentum is identical for both objects but opposite in sign. The subsection explicitly states that momentum changes of interacting objects cancel each other out, so the total change of momentum of the system is zero, meaning the total momentum before and after a collision remains the same. This relationship generalizes to N interacting objects: the total momentum of a system of N interacting objects is constant in time and is conserved.

This subsection introduces the energy conditions for circular orbits, establishing that objects are gravitationally bound when total energy is negative. Key quantities include kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, and total energy; the subsection derives relationships by applying Newton's second law to circular motion and multiplying by orbital radius r. The central relationships are: total energy equals the sum of kinetic and potential energies; total energy is negative with magnitude equal to the kinetic energy; and the magnitude of kinetic energy is exactly one-half the magnitude of potential energy. These energy relationships apply to any two masses in circular orbits about their common center of mass at distance r. Students would search for: gravitationally bound objects, circular orbits, kinetic energy in orbits, potential energy in orbits, total energy in orbits, and the virial relationship between kinetic and potential energy.

This subsection establishes the two requirements for momentum conservation in a system: (1) the mass of the system must remain constant during interaction, with any mass transferred between objects balanced so total mass is unchanged, and (2) the net external force on the system must be zero. The subsection explains that internal forces—those between objects within the system—cannot change total momentum because each force is balanced by an equal and opposite force, causing momentum changes to cancel; however, external forces (such as gravity or friction) change the system's total momentum. A system meeting both requirements is defined as a closed system (or isolated system), and the principle governing such systems is the Law of Conservation of Momentum, which states that total momentum of a system of N interacting objects remains constant in time. The subsection clarifies that external forces may act on a system provided they cancel to produce zero net external force, as exemplified by billiard balls where weight forces are balanced by normal forces.

summary: This subsection introduces the displacement vector in multidimensional motion by first establishing that particle position in three dimensions is described using coordinates x, y, and z, expressed as a position vector r from the origin, with these coordinates as functions of time t in a right-handed coordinate system. This subsection categorizes collision and explosion types by how momentum and kinetic energy behave. **Elastic collisions** occur when two or more objects bounce off each other; momentum is conserved and kinetic energy is conserved. **Inelastic collisions** occur when objects collide and stick together, forming a composite object; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy decreases. **Perfectly inelastic collisions** represent the maximum loss of kinetic energy, occurring when objects stick together and remain motionless. **Explosions** occur when a single object breaks apart into multiple pieces; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy increases (supplied by conversion of potential energy—chemical, elastic, or other forms). The subsection establishes that in a closed system, momentum is always conserved, but kinetic energy may or may not be conserved depending on collision type. This subsection analyzes a car-truck collision using conservation of momentum and the work-energy theorem to determine the car's initial speed. subsection_title: Time of Flight, Trajectory, and Range
summary: This subsection introduces three key quantities for projectile motion on a flat horizontal surface: **time of flight**, **trajectory**, and **range**. Time of flight is derived from kinematic equations by setting vertical displacement to zero and is linearly proportional to initial velocity in the y direction and inversely proportional to g. The trajectory is found by eliminating time t from kinematic equations, yielding the parabolic equation y = (tan θ)x - (g x²)/(2v₀² cos² θ), with coefficients a = tan θ and b = -g/(2v₀² cos² θ). Range (horizontal distance traveled) is derived by setting y = 0 in the trajectory equation and is directly proportional to the square of initial speed and inversely proportional to acceleration of gravity; range is maximum at 45° launch angle. The textbook emphasizes these equations apply only when launch and impact occur on the same horizontal surface, and that complementary launch angles summing to 90° produce equal ranges. Students searching for **kinematic equations**, **projectile motion on flat surfaces**, **parabolic trajectory**, **launch angle**, **initial velocity**, and **gravity's effect on range** would find this content.

Einstein's theory of special relativity (1905) establishes that the speed of light is the universal speed limit, which has profound consequences: space and time are no longer absolute, and observers in relative motion disagree on length and time measurements. This speed limit challenges two key assumptions in Newton's law of gravitation: (1) that gravity is an action-at-a-distance force—meaning changes in one mass's position are instantly communicated to all other masses without physical contact—and (2) that the masses in Newton's law of gravitation are identical to those in Newton's second law, an assumption verified experimentally but lacking first-principle justification. Einstein's general relativity (1916) addressed both issues by reconceptualizing gravity not as a force but as a theory of space-time geometry, describing how mass and acceleration distort and interact with space-time. Search terms: special relativity, speed of light, space and time, action-at-a-distance force, Newton's law of gravitation, gravitational mass, inertial mass, general relativity, space-time geometry.

This subsection establishes that conservation of momentum and conservation of energy are fundamental to understanding atomic and subatomic particles through collision experiments. It describes the Rutherford scattering experiment (1909), in which Ernest Rutherford, Hans Geiger, and Ernest Marsden bombarded a thin sheet of gold foil with high-energy alpha-particles (helium nuclei) and detected their subsequent velocities. The textbook contrasts competing atomic models—Thomson's uniform charge distribution, Lewis's regular polygon arrangement, and Nagaoka's nuclear model—and explains how each predicted different deflection patterns for alpha-particles. The actual experimental results showed that nearly all alpha-particles passed through undeflected, while those that were deflected underwent large-angle deflections, some reversing direction completely (180°), contradicting all existing models. Rutherford used conservation of momentum and conservation of energy as the foundation to develop a new atomic model that better explained these collision observations. This subsection introduces **the principle of equivalence** and its corollary, foundational concepts in Einstein's general theory of gravitation. The principle of equivalence states that free fall and weightlessness are indistinguishable; there is no difference between them in Einstein's framework. The corollary establishes that a uniform gravitational field and uniform acceleration in the absence of gravity produce identical physical effects and are experimentally indistinguishable—experiments performed in a laboratory on Earth (where the gravitational field is essentially uniform) yield identical results to those in a laboratory accelerating in deep space away from all masses. The subsection reframes gravitation itself: gravitation is not a force between two objects but rather the result of each object responding to the effect the other has on space-time surrounding it. A uniform gravitational field and uniform acceleration have exactly the same effect on space-time. **Search terms:** principle of equivalence, free fall, weightlessness, uniform gravitational field, uniform acceleration, space-time, general theory of gravitation.
